title: England's Case for Math Automaticity
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman revisits Jo Boaler's 2015 prediction that England's requirement to memorize times tables by age 9 would produce anxious, disengaged students while America's shift away from rote practice under Common Core would pay off, and shows that a decade of PISA and TIMSS results has produced the opposite result. England has held roughly steady on both tests while US scores have fallen sharply, with the widest US decline occurring on TIMSS, the curriculum-sensitive test most likely to reflect what is actually taught in classrooms. Aldeman argues Boaler's framing sets fact fluency and conceptual understanding up as competitors when cognitive science treats them as complementary, since automatic recall of basic facts frees working memory for the harder reasoning Boaler wants students to do. He grounds this in the 2008 National Mathematics Advisory Panel's conclusion that computational facility and conceptual understanding jointly support problem solving, and closes by noting many US children never reach fluent recall at all. The piece functions as a data-driven rebuttal of a specific, once-influential curriculum claim, using England as a real-world natural experiment against the policy path Boaler recommended.
points: Treats England versus the US as an unplanned decade-long natural experiment on math automaticity, using two independently designed international tests (PISA and TIMSS) rather than a single data source to guard against test-specific artifacts.

Highlights that the widest US decline shows up specifically on TIMSS, the curriculum-aligned test most sensitive to classroom practice, which undercuts the idea that skills-based US instruction was protecting reasoning ability while sacrificing rote fluency.

Reframes fact fluency and conceptual understanding as complementary rather than competing goods, arguing automaticity exists precisely to free working memory capacity for the multistep reasoning that skills-first advocates prize.

Anchors the cognitive-science claim in the 2008 National Mathematics Advisory Panel's finding that computational facility with whole numbers rests on automatic recall of basic facts, not on avoiding it.

Names the specific, falsifiable prediction Boaler made in 2015 and shows it did not materialize, modeling how a decade-old curriculum argument can be tested against real outcome data rather than re-litigated on theory alone.
quotes: Boaler wrote that this requirement would result in rising levels of math anxiety and students turning away from mathematics in record numbers, while the US, moving in the opposite direction under Common Core, would de-emphasize rote memorization.
But a decade of international exams now show the opposite. England's scores have held relatively stable, while scores in the U.S., which moved in the direction Boaler recommended, have declined.
In 2015, England and the United States were literally tied on the TIMSS 8th grade math test. By 2023, England's scores had risen 7 points while here in the States scores fell by 30 points.

If England's times table memorization requirement was producing brittle, anxious students who couldn't think flexibly, you might expect to see England underperforming on PISA relative to TIMSS. But English students are performing well on both sets of tests, and the curriculum-based test, the one most sensitive to what gets taught and practiced in the classroom, is where the US declines have been the steepest.

Boaler's 2015 paper is framed as if math instruction is either about drilling facts or developing number sense, and she believes that the former can crowd out and even harm the latter. But that is a false choice.
The basic reason math fact fluency matters is that it frees up brainpower to do more complex mathematical work, like figuring out how to solve a multistep word problem.
Conceptual understanding of mathematical operations, fluent execution of procedures, and fast access to number combinations together support effective and efficient problem solving.

Ten years ago, Boaler predicted that England's emphasis on memorizing multiplication facts would produce rising math anxiety and drive students away from mathematics. The disaster Boaler predicted has not materialized.
